messages.subject: Is there way to determine abundances differences between three treatments?
messages.subject_clean: Is there way to determine abundances differences between three treatments?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I apologize if this is a simple answer, but so far I am stumped. For my study I have three treatments (Control, HC, and SI) in a random block design where I conducted point counts 5 times in both 2016 and 2017. I used gdistsamp (stacking the data to account for multiple years) to model the effect of treatment on species abundances, and tested the goodness of fit for each model with 100 simulations.

Now that I have predicted abundances for each treatment is there a way to compare the abundances between all three treatments? Control is the intercept for my models, so I can see if there is a difference between Control and HC and then between Control and SI, but I haven't found any way to compare HC and SI directly. I have plotted my predicted values with confidence intervals, but I'm not sure there is a solid way to determine if they are significantly different from one another. Is there something simple I am missing?

Here is an example of my model and predicted abundances from one species if that helps.

> coye.trt.obs2

messages.body_plain:
Here's a partial answer to get you started. This  <https://stats.stackexchange.com/a/60821/45889>gives a good overview of what's happening with categorical predictors in linear models, but it sounds like you already understand most (or all) of that. What you want is contrasts. Here's  <https://stats.idre.ucla.edu/r/faq/how-can-i-test-contrasts-in-r/>an overview of contrasts in R. Unfortunately, I'm not really going to answer your question because I'm not sure if/how you would implement contrasts in unmarked.

One work-around is to set either HC or SI as the first factor level (so that it's treated as the intercept) and run a 2nd model. Another work-around is to run a model without an intercept. This would increase the number of parameters in the model by 1. Instead of estimating 2 effects (difference between level 1 and level 2; difference between level 1 and level 3), the model would estimate 3 effects (mean of control, mean of HC, mean of SI). You could then see whether or not the confidence intervals for the mean of each of the treatments overlap.

from 23-25 April 2018 Michael Schaub and I are hosting a Nimble introductory workshop taught by Perry de Valpine (University of California, Berkeley), see attachment and also here: http://www.phidot.org/forum/viewtopic.php?f=8&t=3586

Nimble is the latest member of the software family for fitting hierarchical models that uses the BUGS language to describe the model. In our opinion this is almost a prerequisite for wide adoption by ecologist and other non-statisticians. Nimble offers exciting capabilities to extend the functionality, customize the MCMC samplers and allows fitting of hierarchical models by likelihood methods.

Best regards  --- Marc Kéry

Hello there! I have been running into problems trying to create an unmarkedMultFrame. I keep getting the error message: obsCovData does not have M*obsNum rows, when I try to create the UMF. I would appreciate any help, as I am fairly new to R and have tried several options (list(), as.vector(), etc.) outlined in previous posts. Thank you - Sean.

My code:

#EH Data
y <- FosnEH[,2:15] #Detection History
n <- nrow(FosnEH) #Number of Sites
J <- 7 #Number of Site Visits per Site (secondary sampling occasions)
T <- 2 #Number of Years (primary sampling occasions)

#Year Effects
years.cov <- data.frame(matrix(rep(2016:2017, each = n), n, T))
years.cov <- data.frame(lapply(years.cov, as.factor))

#Site Covariates
site.alias <- data.frame(site.alias=FosnEH[,1]) #Site
site.region <- data.frame(site.region=FosnEH[,16]) #Region
site.elev <- data.frame(site.elev=FosnEH[,17]) #Elevation

#Combine Site Covarites
site.covs <- data.frame(c(site.alias,site.region,site.elev))

#Observation Covariates
obs.visit <- data.frame(FosnEH[,18:31]) #Site Visit Number
obs.dayscore <- data.frame(FosnEH[,32:45]) #Dayscore of Visit

#Combine Obs covariates
obs.covs <- data.frame(c(obs.visit,obs.dayscore))

#Create UMF
FosnUMF <- unmarkedMultFrame(y = y, siteCovs = site.covs, obsCovs = obs.covs, numPrimary = 2, yearlySiteCovs = years.cov)

Error in validObject(.Object) :
  invalid class “unmarkedFrame” object: obsCovData does not have M*obsNum rows.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all.

I forward a short description of the capabilities of the new Nimble software just posted in the HMecology google group.

Best regards  --- Marc

From: Perry de Valpine [pdeva...@berkeley.edu]
Sent: 12 January 2018 18:51
To: Tomas Telensky
Cc: Kery Marc; hmec...@googlegroups.com; unmarked
Subject: Re: Introductory NIMBLE Workshop, Switzerland, April 2018

In a nutshell: NIMBLE makes both the BUGS model language and algorithms that use models extensible.  You can add new functions and distributions.  You can customize choice of samplers, write new samplers, and write/use other methods (not just MCMC).  Models and algorithms are compiled by generating and compiling C++, so everything can run fast.  We do have relatively new support for CAR models, and there is room for anyone to contribute improved general or case-specific methods.  If you write something that you want to share, you can contribute to NIMBLE or write your own R package that uses NIMBLE.  Something like BART regression trees would be an interesting case for adding new functions, distributions and samplers to support these models.  If there are external libraries you want to use, you can have the compiled NIMBLE code call externally compiled code.  For more information (including a full user manual), please see http:r-nimble.org <http://r-nimble.org>

While I have the floor: we are hiring a post-doc!  Please see https://r-nimble.org/nimble-has-a-post-doc-or-software-developer-position-open

Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sean,

You are correct that 0.619 is the estimate of the proportion of sites occupied in the sample. However, it’s a bit trickier to get the CIs because you need to condition on the observed data. One option is to simulate the latent occupancy state from the estimated posterior distributions. You can then compute summary statistics from these simulated values. For the occupancy case, you can simulate with a binomial distribution, like this:
library(unmarked)
example(occu)

pmean <- bup(re, stat="mean") # Posterior mean

nSites <- length(pmean)
nSim <- 1000
z <- matrix(NA, nSites, nSim)
for(i in 1:nSim) {
    z[,i] <- rbinom(nSites, 1, pmean) # Simulated occupancy states
    }
N <- colSums(z) # number of sites occupied in each simulation

quantile(N, c(0.025, 0.975))/nSites # 95% CI

I might add some functions to do this in a more general way for each model in unmarked.

Richard

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I had a question about offsets and how to implement them in gdistsamp. I'm using gdistsamp to calculate the density of a species. I conducted 100m radius PCs (binned every 10m for Unmarked) and 12 sites 7 times throughout the summer. Currently in the example I'm going to show, all 100m radius point counts in this example are treated as having equal area. Just for context there are experimental treatments I included in the phiformula model for each of these.

area <- pi*100^2/10000

I decided to run a model calculating density without using an offset given this conversation: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/unmarked/offset%7Csort:date/unmarked/SAKKFOYnO3A/vLBCcBdrCgAJ <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/unmarked/offset%7Csort:date/unmarked/SAKKFOYnO3A/vLBCcBdrCgAJ.> as it was mentioned that "The output="density" option includes the area offset automatically."

This is the model and first row from predicted density results from that.

i1 <- gdistsamp(lambdaformula= ~Treatment, phiformula= ~1, pformula = ~1, keyfun="hazard", output="density",unitsOut="ha", se=TRUE,K=50, data = df)
newdata_trtdense <- data.frame(Treatment= as.factor(c("A", "B", "C")))
predict_dense<-predict(i1, type="lambda", newdata=newdata_trtdense, appedData=T)
predict_dense$Playback<-paste(newdata_trtdense$Playback)

i1 - density without offset
Treatment      Predicted         SE               lower          upper
      A             1.867042     0.6251729    0.9685719   3.598953

I figured the predicted value must represent 1.867042 birds/total area in hectares (1.86/ha is too high). So I thought if I divided it by the area, I would get the appropriate density I wanted which is 0.5945994/ha. (This seems closer to reality).

I also thought that calculating the abundance should give me the same thing if that's what the output of the density was. However, abundance gave me the following result:

i2 <- gdistsamp(lambdaformula= ~Treatment, phiformula= ~1, pformula = ~1, keyfun="hazard", output="abund", se=TRUE,K=50, data = df)
newdata_trtabund <- data.frame(Treatment= as.factor(c("A", "B", "C")))
predict_abund<-predict(i2, type="lambda", newdata=newdata_trtabund, appedData=T)
predict_abund$Playback<-paste(newdata_trtabund$Playback)

i2 - abundance without offset
Treatment      Predicted         SE               lower          upper
      A            1.058828      0.5286693    0.3979453   2.817264

Dividing the predicted value by the area this time gives me a density of 0.3370354, not the same as my density results

Just out of curiosity I wanted to see what would happen with an offset for area included since I realized I'm unsure as to what output I'm receiving. I ran both density and abundance models again with the only difference this time being the inclusion of the log(offset(area)) in lambda.

i3 <- gdistsamp(lambdaformula= ~Treatment, phiformula= ~1+log(offset(area)), pformula = ~1, keyfun="hazard", output="density",unitsOut="ha", se=TRUE,K=50, data = df)
newdata_trtdenseoff <- data.frame(Treatment= as.factor(c("A", "B", "C")))
predict_denseoff<-predict(i3, type="lambda", newdata=newdata_trtdenseoff, appedData=T)
predict_denseoff$Playback<-paste(newdata_trtdenseoff$Playback)

i3 - density with offset
Treatment      Predicted         SE               lower          upper
      A             0.3272650   0.1647852    0.1219834   0.8780079

i4 <- gdistsamp(lambdaformula= ~Treatment, phiformula= ~1+log(offset(area)), pformula = ~1, keyfun="hazard", output="abund", se=TRUE,K=50, data = df)
newdata_trtabundoff <- data.frame(Treatment= as.factor(c("A", "B", "C")))
predict_abundoff<-predict(i4, type="lambda", newdata=newdata_trtabundoff, appedData=T)
predict_abundoff$Playback<-paste(newdata_trtabundoff$Playback)

i4 - abundance with offset
Treatment      Predicted         SE               lower          upper
      A             1.028057     0.5176523    0.3831916   2.758153

i3 is equal to i4 divided by the area. That makes sense and it seems like including the offset is the way to go.

However I suppose I'm a little confused as to what my outputs are and I have a few questions:

1) Since the output="density" option includes the area offset automatically, what is the reason for the different results between i1 and i3/why does i1 have such a large number? i3 seems a lot closer to correct when considering the #birds that I was aware of in these plots and considering the abundance output.

2) Since the abundance is the amount of birds per site area (so here 100m radius), why does adding an offset change the values? Does abundance behave differently than density in terms of needing to define the area?

3) What is the offset/lack of offset doing to the results in each of these contexts and what is the correct practice (i.e. is it prudent to always include the offset whether the area is constant or not, or are there situations where you might not want to include an offset for area/size of site)?

I hope the above is clear and that my questions make sense.

I greatly appreciate any insight that you have.

Much appreciated.

Stephen

Matt is correct. You have built a model that estimates the expected occupancy state based on multiple variables (2 in your case). So, to create a prediction,  you must provide values for both. newdata.1<-data.frame(turb=seq(min(cadframe&turb),max(cadframe$turb),length=50), cond=mean(cadframe$cond))

Hi Matt and Chris, and anyone else following this thread,

I am unsure if this is the correct way to do this. For example, below I coded my dataframe based on Chris' suggestion. I modified the code slightly because it would not let me use the "$" symbol as an operator:

> cadframe$turb
Error in cadframe$turb : $ operator not defined for this S4 class

Here is the code I used:

> newdata.1<-data.frame(cond=seq(-1,4, by=0.01),turb=turb.mean)
> fm2.p<-predict(fm2,type="det",newdata=newdata.1,appendData=TRUE)
> head(fm2.p)
     Predicted           SE        lower        upper  cond    turb
1 2.200753e-32 4.447902e-31 1.377495e-49 3.516030e-15 -1.00 11.7906
2 2.172725e-32 4.391163e-31 1.361084e-49 3.468364e-15 -0.99 11.7906
3 2.145054e-32 4.335148e-31 1.344867e-49 3.421349e-15 -0.98 11.7906
4 2.117736e-32 4.279848e-31 1.328840e-49 3.374977e-15 -0.97 11.7906
5 2.090765e-32 4.225254e-31 1.313002e-49 3.329239e-15 -0.96 11.7906
6 2.064138e-32 4.171356e-31 1.297351e-49 3.284126e-15 -0.95 11.7906
>

Doing so gives unrealistic predicted values and the graph looks like a straight line at Y=0.

I think setting the mean value to zero messes with the predict() function equation I mentioned above, where it is using the beta values (coefficients) to make predictions, which I will post again here:

Logit (p) =Β(intercept) +B(turb)* turb +B(cond)*cond

Site x (p)= exp(Β(intercept) +B(turb)* turb +B(cond)*cond)/(1+exp(Β(intercept) +B(turb)* turb +B(cond)*cond)

For example, I believe the predict function is looking for values of both turbidity and conductivity based on the above equation, and setting one to the mean is skewing the predicted values.

If you only set the dataframe to include one of the covariates, it throws an error code that it can't find the other:

> newdata.1<-data.frame(cond=seq(-1,4, by=0.01))

> fm2.p<-predict(fm2,type="det",newdata=newdata.1,appendData=TRUE)

Error in eval(predvars, data, env) : object 'turb' not found

> newdata.1<-data.frame(turb=seq(-1,10, by=0.01))
> fm2.p<-predict(fm2,type="det",newdata=newdata.1,appendData=TRUE)

Error in eval(predvars, data, env) : object 'cond' not found

So, with the same goal in mind to graph separate detection curves for each covariate based on the additive model for detection probability:

 fm2<-occu(~turb + cond ~fcover,cadframe)

Is there currently no way to graph separate detection curves from an additive model using the unmarked functions?

Should I simply try to do the equation by hand in R by removing the values being multiplied by the coefficient of the covariate I am not interested in graphing?

For example, If I am interested in graphing a detection curve for turbidity, would I modify the above equation to read:

Site x (p)= exp(Β(intercept) +B(turb)* turb +B(cond))/(1+exp(Β(intercept) +B(turb)* turb +B(cond))

where the values for conductivity are removed?

Thanks,

-Sean

messages.body_plain:
Dear unmarked community,

I need advise on determining the type of model that would help take the most advantage of my data.

I conducted bird point counts in 100 sites, using circular plots of 50m and grouping birds into two distance bins (0-25m, 25-50m).

I visited each site one time. On each visit I conducted three consecutive 6 minutes point counts. Therefore, I counted bird for 18 minutes total.

One option I am exploring is to use a time-removal framework. However, my design technically is not time removal because in the field I counted all birds again on each point count. I did not discard a bird that I counted on time 1 during time 2. But to build the data frame for time removal, I would assume that if I have the same number of bird on each time, then they are the same individuals in both counts.

Does anyone have tried this?

What could be the limitation of this approach?

I will appreciate your comments and advise,

Isabel

messages.subject_clean: application of a time-removal model on consecutive point counts data.
messages.body_plain:
Hi Isabel,

I wouldn't fit a time-removal model, for reasons that you bring up. Instead, I think that I would just use the Binomial N-mixture model (fit in unmarked with the pcount function). The data (repeated counts) more or less directly align with the likelihood of that model; that these are repeated intervals over one visit rather than repeated visits with a single interval shouldn't really matter other than changing how one might think about interpreting and modeling variation in N. For example, something like Julian Date might make more sense as a covariate for lambda here rather than a covariate for p, as it might traditionally be used.

I guess you could theoretically fit a generalized distance sampling model, but with two bins, I'm not sure you'd be able to meaningfully estimate detection parameters.

Cheers,

John
